title: Harry Kane Eyes NFL Kicking Career After Soccer
summary:
Harry Kane has scored 85 goals for England — more than any other player in the country's history. But the 33-year-old striker is already thinking about what comes next. And it's not golf. It's American football.

Speaking at England's UEFA Nations League training camp on Wednesday, Kane said he is seriously considering a future as an NFL kicker. "That is something I will try and look at a bit more seriously," he said. "It all depends on what happens in my career over the next five or six years. The NFL is a lot more realistic than the golf one, let's put it that way."

Kane, who plays for Bayern Munich, believes his penalty-taking experience gives him a head start. He has converted 25 penalties for England. "I take penalties and it is a very similar pressure and technique," he said. "In terms of training, I would be closer to that more than any other sport."

But he knows switching sports isn't easy. "With all elite sports, when you watch it on TV, people make it look easy; you think it is possible, but that is not always the case," Kane said. He added that if he did try, he would take six months to a year to practise beforehand.

Kane also mentioned a possible move to MLS, the top American soccer league. "Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with the seasons," he said.

Some athletes have already made the jump. Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey was a first-round MLS draft pick by Toronto FC in 2017, though he never played for the first team. Jake Bates also played college football before becoming a kicker for the Detroit Lions.

For now, Kane's focus remains on soccer. Talks over a new contract at Bayern are progressing. "We're in good talks," he said. "There's still some things that we need to iron out. I'm happy there. I think it won't be too long before there's some sort of announcement."
why_it_matters: It is a window into how professional athletes plan for short careers and how specialised skills can transfer between sports — and it raises bigger questions about how teams identify and develop narrow roles like the kicker.

background_read: Harry Kane (England's captain and all-time record goal-scorer, now playing for the German club Bayern Munich) broke Wayne Rooney's England scoring record in 2023 and is also Tottenham's record scorer. The penalty — a free shot from twelve yards with only the goalkeeper to beat — is the closest thing in soccer to an American football field goal, because both demand a repeatable technique under extreme pressure.

The NFL (National Football League, the top level of American football in the United States) uses a specialist kicker for field goals and extra points. Because kicking depends more on technique than speed or size, kickers often keep playing into their late thirties — much longer than most other players — which is part of why a late switch between sports is not unthinkable. MLS (Major League Soccer) is the top U.S. soccer league and runs on a different calendar from Europe's leagues, which is why Kane mentioned possibly combining the two.

Athletes switching sports is rare but real: Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey was a first-round MLS draft pick by Toronto FC in 2017, and Jake Bates kicked in college before joining the Detroit Lions. Their careers show that the specific, repetitive skill of kicking can transfer across sports — but also that it takes years of specialised practice to reach the professional level.

perspectives.description: They point out that penalty-taking is a repetitive, pressure-filled skill that closely resembles kicking a field goal. Precedents like Brandon Aubrey and Jake Bates show that non-traditional routes into the NFL can work. An MLS spell could even let Kane keep playing soccer while he trains as a kicker.

Critics note that elite kicking is a full-time craft with its own techniques, snap timing and snap-holder chemistry that take years to master. At the age Kane would arrive, his window would be short, and any failure would be very public. Some also suspect the talk is playful and that his commitment to Bayern and England comes first.

They observe that cross-sport switches succeed most often in closed, technical roles such as kicking, goalkeeping or sprinting, where raw athletic variety matters less. Career length also matters: kickers can last far longer than outfield players, which changes the maths of a late switch. Historically, though, such conversions remain rare and highly selective.

The next visible steps will be his Bayern contract announcement and whether a future MLS move actually happens. If it does, the overlapping seasons could make a dual-sport attempt logistically possible in a way it never was before. Either way, his comments push teams to think harder about recruiting kicking talent from outside American football.
